title: Keystone Species
subject: eco
paras: In an arch made of stones, the keystone is the wedge-shaped stone at the top. If it is removed, the whole arch falls. In the 1960s, the ecologist Robert Paine borrowed this word to describe certain animals that hold their ecosystems together.

Paine studied rocky shores on the coast of Washington State. There, a sea star called Pisaster eats mussels. In one experiment, Paine removed all the sea stars from a section of shore and left a nearby section alone for comparison.

The results were striking. Without sea stars, mussels spread quickly and covered the rocks. They crowded out seaweeds, barnacles, and snails that had lived there before. Within a few years, the number of species in the area fell sharply. In the section with sea stars, the variety of life stayed high.

Paine concluded that a keystone species has an effect far larger than its numbers would suggest. Sea stars were not the most common animals on the shore, but by eating mussels, they made room for many other species.

Since then, scientists have identified other keystone species. Sea otters eat sea urchins, which would otherwise destroy kelp forests. Wolves in Yellowstone National Park affect the behavior of elk, which in turn affects plants along rivers. Protecting such species can help protect entire ecosystems.
